title: Intrinsic value and time value
teaches: In, at and out of the money; intrinsic value is what the option would be worth if it expired right now, and the rest of the premium is time value that melts to zero by expiry.

sources.publisher: The Options Clearing Corporation and the US options exchanges
sources.title: Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options (June 2024 edition)
sources.why_reliable: The official options disclosure document every options customer must receive (June 2024 edition, the version Cboe Regulatory Circular RC24-009 says replaces all prior ones). theocc.com refuses plain clients (403), so this cites the copy Robinhood distributes to its customers (cover: June 2024; copyright the exchanges and OCC).

facts.quote: An option’s premium has two main components: intrinsic value and time value (also known as extrinsic value).
facts.claim: Every option premium is intrinsic value plus time value; time value is also called extrinsic value.

facts.quote: A call option is in-the-money when the underlying security's price is higher than the strike price.
facts.claim: A call is in the money when the stock is above the strike.

facts.quote: A put option is in-the-money if the underlying security's price is less than the strike price. Only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.
facts.claim: A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike, and only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.

facts.quote: Time value is any premium in excess of intrinsic value before expiration.
facts.claim: Time value is whatever the premium is above intrinsic value.

facts.quote: The longer the amount of time available for market conditions to work to an investor's benefit, the greater the time value.
facts.claim: More time left to expiry means more time value.

facts.quote: The effect of implied volatility can be difficult to quantify. It can significantly affect the time value portion of an option's premium.
facts.claim: Implied volatility can move the time value part of the premium a lot.

facts.quote: Higher volatility estimates indicate greater expected fluctuations (in either direction) in underlying price levels. This expectation generally results in higher option premiums for puts and calls alike.
facts.claim: When bigger moves are expected, calls and puts both get more expensive.

facts.quote: This term means that the current market value of the underlying interest is the same as the exercise price of the option.
facts.claim: At the money means the stock price equals the strike.

facts.quote: If the current market price of XYZ stock is $43, an XYZ 40 call would be in the money by $3.
facts.claim: With the stock at 43, the 40 call is in the money by 3.

facts.quote: the intrinsic value reflects the amount, if any, by which the option is in the money. An option that is out of the money would have an intrinsic value of zero.
facts.claim: Intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount, and it is zero for an out-of-the-money option.

facts.quote: Time value is whatever the premium of the option is in addition to its intrinsic value. Time value is that part of the premium that reflects the time remaining before expiration.
facts.claim: Time value is the premium minus intrinsic value; it reflects the time left before expiry.

facts.quote: market price of XYZ stock at $45 a share, an XYZ 40 call may have a current market price of $6 a share, reflecting an intrinsic value of $5 a share and a time value of $1 a share
facts.claim: Stock at 45, the 40 call at 6 is 5 of intrinsic value plus 1 of time value.

facts.quote: At a time when the market price of XYZ stock is $40 a share, an XYZ 40 call may have a current market price of, say, $2 a share. This is entirely time value.
facts.claim: An at-the-money call's whole price is time value.

facts.quote: all else remaining the same, the time value of an option usually decreases as the option approaches expiration, and this decrease accelerates as the time to expiration shortens.
facts.claim: Time value shrinks toward expiry, and the shrinking speeds up near the end.

facts.quote: An option normally has very little time value if it is substantially in the money.
facts.claim: A deep in-the-money option usually carries very little time value.

facts.quote: All else being the same, options on more volatile interests command higher premiums than options on less volatile interests.
facts.claim: Options on jumpier stocks cost more, all else equal.

facts.quote: closing transactions may provide an opportunity for an option holder to realize the remaining time value (described below) of the option that would be lost in an exercise.
facts.claim: Selling an option collects its remaining time value; exercising it throws that time value away.

facts.quote: An American-style option may ordinarily be expected to trade for no less than its intrinsic value prior to its expiration, although occasionally an American-style option will trade at less than its intrinsic value.
facts.claim: An American-style option usually trades at or above intrinsic value, but occasionally below it.

facts.quote: Because of an all cash merger involving XYZ Corporation, the stock held by XYZ’s owners is extinguished in return for a payment of $50 in cash per XYZ share.
facts.claim: In the example, an all-cash merger turns each share into 50 dollars of cash.

facts.quote: As a result, an XYZ call option with an exercise price of $40 will lose all of its time value and the option’s value will only reflect the intrinsic value of $10 ($50 – $40 = $10).
facts.claim: After that cash adjustment, the 40 call loses all its time value and is worth its 10 of intrinsic value.

facts.quote: Additionally, an XYZ call option with an exercise price of $60 will become worthless because the exercise price exceeds the $50 cash settlement delivery amount.
facts.claim: A call struck above the cash amount, like the 60 call, becomes worthless.

facts.quote: an option holder must not only be right about the direction of an anticipated price change in the underlying interest, but she must also be right about when the price change will occur.
facts.claim: An option buyer has to be right on direction and on timing.

facts.quote: The more an option is out of the money and the shorter the remaining time to expiration, the greater the risk that an option holder will lose all or part of his investment in the option.
facts.claim: Further out of the money and less time left means a bigger risk of losing the premium.

facts.quote: an XYZ 50 call (covering 100 shares of XYZ at a premium of $5 a share)
facts.claim: In the example, the 50 call costs 5 a share.

facts.quote: would incur a 20% loss even if the price of XYZ increased to 54 (assuming he did not sell his options while they had significant remaining time value)
facts.claim: Holding the 50 calls bought at 5 to expiry with the stock at 54 still loses 20%.

facts.quote: Upon expiration, an option has no time value and is worth its intrinsic value only.
facts.claim: At expiry an option has no time value left and is worth only its intrinsic value.

facts.quote: options that are either deep-in-the-money or far out-of-the-money will have very little decay as they have less time premium.
facts.claim: Deep in-the-money and far out-of-the-money options carry less time value than at-the-money ones.

facts.quote: Theta or time decay is not linear. The theoretical rate of decay will tend to increase as time to expiration decreases.
facts.claim: Time decay is not a straight line; it speeds up as expiry approaches.

facts.quote: When an investor exercises a call option, the net price paid for the underlying stock on a per share basis is the sum of the call's strike price plus the premium paid for the call.
facts.claim: A call buyer's real cost for the shares is strike plus premium, which is the break-even at expiry.

facts.quote: The terms “in the money” and “out of the money” refer to the option contract itself and do not represent the profitability of your trade, nor does it depend on whether you have bought or written the option.
facts.claim: In the money describes the contract, not whether your trade is profitable.

facts.quote: When an option contract expires, the time value would be zero. At this point the option value is equal to the intrinsic value.
facts.claim: At expiry, time value is zero and the option is worth its intrinsic value.

facts.quote: The time value of an option (before its expiration date) will always be greatest when the option is at the money.
facts.claim: Time value is greatest at the money.

facts.quote: Intrinsic value does not mean profit.
facts.claim: Having intrinsic value is not the same as making money on the trade.

facts.quote: an option with one month to expiration that is out of the money will have more extrinsic value than an out-of-the-money option with one week to expiration.
facts.claim: The same out-of-the-money option has more time value with a month left than with a week left.

facts.quote: Options buyers focus on the ask price as it represents the cost and risk of purchasing an option.
facts.claim: A buyer pays the ask, so the ask is the buyer's real cost.

facts.quote: Generally, options with further expiration dates cost more than an equivalent option with a shorter expiration date.
facts.claim: The later expiry usually costs more than the same option with an earlier expiry.

facts.quote: ATM options have the largest amount of extrinsic value of any option.
facts.claim: At-the-money options carry the most time value.

facts.quote: buyers suffer from the loss of extrinsic value while option sellers benefit from this loss
facts.claim: Time value melting away hurts the buyer and helps the seller.

facts.quote: OTM options prices are entirely made up of extrinsic value.
facts.claim: An out-of-the-money option's price is all time value.

facts.quote: If the stock price is exactly equal to the strike price, the contract is ATM and has no intrinsic value.
facts.claim: Stock exactly at the strike is at the money, with no intrinsic value.

facts.quote: substantially out of the money has only time value, the amount of that time value is normally less than the time value of an option having the same underlying interest and expiration that is at the money.
facts.claim: A far out-of-the-money option is all time value, but normally less of it than the at-the-money option, same stock and same expiry.

walkthroughs.title: Two parts in every premium
steps: Every option price has two parts: intrinsic value and time value.
Intrinsic value is how far the option is in the money right now.
Time value is everything you pay on top of that.
Stock at $45, the 40 call at $6. That's $5 of intrinsic value and $1 of time value.

walkthroughs.title: In, at and out of the money
steps: A call is in the money when the stock is above the strike.
A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike.
Stock right at the strike is at the money.
Only in-the-money options have intrinsic value. Everything else has zero.

walkthroughs.title: The clock on time value
steps: All else equal, time value shrinks as expiry gets closer, and the shrinking speeds up near the end.
At expiry there is no time left. The option is worth its intrinsic value only.
If you're the buyer, time value is the part the clock takes from you.

questions.q: An option's premium is made of two parts. Which two?
questions.why: Intrinsic value and time value. Intrinsic is the in-the-money part, and time value is everything above it.
questions.lesson_line: Premium equals intrinsic value plus time value. Split every quote that way.

wrong.The bid and the ask: Those are the two sides of the quote, what buyers bid and sellers ask. They aren't parts of the price.
wrong.The strike and the expiry: Those are contract terms. They shape the price, but they aren't the pieces it splits into.
wrong.Delta and theta: Those measure how the price changes. They don't split the premium into parts.

questions.q: A put is in the money when the stock trades above its strike.
questions.why: False. A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike. Above the strike, that's a call.
questions.lesson_line: Calls are in the money above the strike. Puts are in the money below it.

questions.q: On an option quote, what does intrinsic value mean?
choices: The amount it is in the money
What the company is really worth
questions.answer: The amount it is in the money
questions.why: The amount it is in the money. Out of the money, intrinsic value is zero.
questions.lesson_line: Intrinsic value is the in-the-money amount. Nothing more.

wrong.The whole premium you pay: The premium is intrinsic value plus time value. Intrinsic is only one part.
wrong.What the company is really worth: That's the stock investor's meaning of the phrase. On an option it's the in-the-money amount.
wrong.The time left until expiry: Time left drives time value, the other part of the premium.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: An out-of-the-money option has ___ intrinsic value.
questions.why: Zero. Intrinsic value is the amount the option is in the money, so out of the money it is zero.
questions.lesson_line: Intrinsic value stops at zero. It never goes negative.

questions.q: Price sits exactly at the option's strike price. What do you call that option?
questions.why: At the money. The stock price is the same as the strike, so there is no intrinsic value.
questions.lesson_line: Stock equals strike: at the money, and no intrinsic value.

wrong.In the money: That needs the stock past the strike: above it for a call, below it for a put.
wrong.Out of the money: That needs the stock on the wrong side of the strike. Here it sits right on it.

questions.q: On an option quote, what does time value mean?
choices: The amount it is in the money
The gap from stock to strike
questions.why: The premium above intrinsic value. It's the part of the price that reflects the time left before expiry.
questions.lesson_line: Time value is a dollar amount: the premium minus intrinsic value.

wrong.The days left until expiry: The days left drive time value, but time value is a dollar amount in the premium.
wrong.The amount it is in the money: That's intrinsic value, the other part of the premium.
wrong.The gap from stock to strike: That gap is distance, not price. For an in-the-money option it's the intrinsic value.

questions.q: With the stock at 64, which put is in the money?
questions.why: The 70 put. A put is in the money when the stock is below the strike, and 64 is below 70.
questions.lesson_line: Puts are in the money when the stock sits below the strike.

wrong.The 60 put: The stock is above 60, so this put is out of the money. It's the 60 call that would be in the money.
wrong.The 64 put: The stock is right at 64, so this one is at the money, not in it.

questions.q: An out-of-the-money option's whole premium is time value.
questions.why: True. Out of the money, intrinsic value is zero, so every cent of the premium is time value.
questions.lesson_line: No intrinsic value means the whole price is time.

questions.q: What is an option worth at the moment it expires?
questions.why: Its intrinsic value only. At expiry there is no time left, so there is no time value.
questions.lesson_line: At expiry the time is gone. Only intrinsic value is left.

wrong.What you paid for it: Your cost doesn't set the price. The market only pays for what the option is worth.
wrong.Intrinsic plus a little time: With no time left, time value is zero. Nothing is left to pay for.
wrong.Zero, every option expires dead: Only options with no intrinsic value expire worthless. In-the-money ones are worth their intrinsic value.

questions.q: Same stock, same expiry. Which strike usually holds the most time value?
questions.why: The at-the-money strike. Deep in-the-money and far out-of-the-money options carry less time value.
questions.lesson_line: At the money holds the most time value. Deep in or far out holds little.

wrong.A deep in-the-money strike: Its price is big, but it's mostly intrinsic value. Very little of it is time.
wrong.A far out-of-the-money strike: It's all time value, but only a small amount of it.
wrong.Every strike holds the same: Time value changes with the strike. It peaks near the stock price.

questions.q: The stock trades at 87.50. What is the 80 call's intrinsic value, per share?
questions.why: $7.50. For a call it's stock minus strike: 87.50 minus 80.
questions.lesson_line: Call intrinsic: stock minus strike, never below zero.

questions.q: With the stock at 61, what is the 70 put's intrinsic value, per share?
questions.why: $9. For a put it's strike minus stock: 70 minus 61.
questions.lesson_line: Put intrinsic: strike minus stock, never below zero.

questions.q: If your call is in the money, your trade is making money.
questions.why: False. In the money describes the contract against the strike, not your trade. You still have to cover what you paid.
questions.lesson_line: In the money is about the strike. Profit is about what you paid.

questions.q: Same stock, same 50 strike. One call expires in 30 days, the other in 60. Which usually costs more?
questions.why: The 60-day call. More time to expiry means more time value, and the intrinsic value is the same for both.
questions.lesson_line: More time costs more. You're paying for more chances to be right.

wrong.The 30-day call: Less time left means less time value, so the shorter one is usually cheaper.
wrong.They cost the same: Same strike and stock means the same intrinsic value. The time value is what differs.

questions.q: The stock is at 52. The 50 call costs 3.40. How much of that is time value, per share?
questions.why: $1.40. Intrinsic is 52 minus 50. Take that off the 3.40 and the rest is time value.
questions.lesson_line: Premium minus intrinsic equals time value. Do it on every quote.

questions.story: A stock trades at 38. You look at the 40 call, priced at 1.10. Expiry is three weeks out.
questions.q: How much of the 1.10 is time value?
questions.why: All of it, $1.10. The call is out of the money, so intrinsic is zero and the whole price is time.
questions.lesson_line: Out of the money, every cent of the premium is time value.

wrong.$3.10: That counts the 2 points below the strike as negative intrinsic value. Intrinsic stops at zero.
wrong.$0: Out of the money means no intrinsic value, not no value. The 1.10 is real, and all of it is time.
wrong.$2: That's how far the stock is from the strike. It isn't a part of the price.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: Exercise an option early and you give up its ___ value.
questions.why: Time. Exercising gets you the intrinsic value only. Selling the option also collects whatever time value is left.
questions.lesson_line: With time value left in the bid, I'd sell the option, not exercise it.

questions.story: XYZ trades at 95. You think it breaks lower. The 100 put is offered at 6.20.
questions.q: How much of that 6.20 is time value?
questions.why: $1.20. The put is in the money by 100 minus 95. The rest of the 6.20 is time value.
questions.lesson_line: Put intrinsic is strike minus stock. Time value is whatever sits on top.

wrong.$5: That's the intrinsic value, 100 minus 95. Time value is what's left above it.
wrong.$6.20: That's the whole premium. Only a put with no intrinsic value is all time value.
wrong.$0: That would make all 6.20 intrinsic value. The put is only in the money by 100 minus 95.

questions.q: An option's time value melts at a steady rate from the day you buy it until expiry.
questions.why: False. Time value shrinks as expiry nears, and the shrinking speeds up as the time left gets short.
questions.lesson_line: The clock runs slow at first and fast at the end.

questions.q: The 100 call is 50.40 with the stock at 150. How much time value is in it, per share?
questions.why: $0.40. Intrinsic is 150 minus 100, and only the 0.40 above it is time. Deep in the money, time value runs thin.
questions.lesson_line: Deep in the money, the premium is almost all intrinsic value.

questions.story: You paid 5.00 for the 50 call. On expiry day the stock closes at 54.
questions.q: Your call finished in the money. What did the trade make or lose, per share?
questions.why: Lost $1 a share. The call is worth 54 minus 50 at the bell, but you paid 5.00 for it.
questions.lesson_line: In the money at expiry can still be a loss. The premium is the bar to clear.

wrong.Made $4 a share: That's the intrinsic value at the close. You paid 5.00, so take that off.
wrong.Lost the whole $5: The call finished in the money, so it's worth $4 at the bell, not zero.
wrong.Broke even: Break-even is the strike plus the premium, and 54 falls short of it.

questions.q: The stock is at 45. You buy the 40 call for 6.00. What stock price at expiry gets you back to even?
questions.why: $46. Strike plus premium, 40 plus 6. From 45 the stock must rise $1, which is the time value you paid.
questions.lesson_line: Hold an in-the-money call to expiry and the stock must rise by the time value just to break even.

questions.story: A stock trades at 112.40. The 105 call shows bid 8.90, ask 9.30. You'd buy at the ask.
questions.q: How much time value are you paying for, per share?
questions.why: $1.90. Intrinsic is 112.40 minus 105. You pay 9.30, and everything above intrinsic is time value.
questions.lesson_line: When you buy, measure time value from the ask. That's the price you actually pay.

wrong.$7.40: That's the intrinsic value, 112.40 minus 105. The question asks what you pay above it.
wrong.$9.30: That's the whole premium. Part of it is intrinsic value.
wrong.$1.50: That uses the 8.90 bid. You're buying, so you pay the 9.30 ask.

questions.story: You own a 40 call. The company agrees to an all-cash buyout at $50 a share. The deal closes and your options now deliver the cash.
questions.q: What is your call worth now, per share?
questions.why: $10, intrinsic only. Once the shares become $50 of cash, the call loses all its time value.
questions.lesson_line: A cash buyout erases time value. Your call is worth the cash minus the strike.

wrong.$10 plus its old time value: Cash can't move, so there is nothing left for time value to pay for. It goes to zero.
wrong.Nothing, deals kill options: Only calls struck at or above the $50 cash die, like a 60 call. Yours is struck at 40.
wrong.Whatever it last traded at: Once the shares turn into cash, the call is worth the cash minus the strike. The last trade doesn't matter.

questions.story: A stock trades at 50 and you're bullish. Call A is the 52 strike with two months left. Call B is the 60 strike expiring Friday.
questions.q: Which call is more likely to lose you the whole premium?
choices: Call A, the 52 with two months
About the same, both are calls
questions.why: Call B. The further out of the money and the less time left, the bigger the risk of losing it all.
questions.lesson_line: Far out of the money with days left is the fastest way to lose the whole premium.

wrong.Call A, the 52 with two months: It costs more, but it sits nearer the stock and has far more time to work.
wrong.About the same, both are calls: Distance from the strike and time left both change the risk. B is worse on both.

questions.story: Two stocks both trade at 100. Stock A swings 5% most days. Stock B barely moves. You price the 100 call on each, same expiry.
questions.q: Which call carries more time value?
questions.why: The call on Stock A. All else equal, options on jumpier stocks cost more, and the extra sits in the time value.
questions.lesson_line: Jumpy stocks carry fatter time value. You pay for the movement up front.

wrong.The call on Stock B: A quiet stock gives the option less chance to pay off, so sellers charge less for the time.
wrong.Same strike, same price: Both calls are at the money with zero intrinsic. Expected movement is what differs, and it drives time value.

questions.q: Before expiry, an American-style option can never trade below its intrinsic value.
questions.why: False. It ordinarily trades at or above intrinsic, but the options disclosure document says it occasionally trades below.
questions.lesson_line: Before you sell a deep in-the-money option, check the bid against its intrinsic value.

questions.story: The stock is at 80. You own the 70 call, bid 11.50, with a month left. You want out of the trade.
questions.q: Selling the call beats exercising and selling the shares. By how much, per share?
questions.why: $1.50, the time value. Exercising nets 80 minus 70. Selling the call gets 11.50, time value included. Fees aside.
questions.lesson_line: Selling the option keeps the time value. Exercising throws it away.

wrong.$10, the intrinsic value: That's what exercising nets you: buy at 70, sell at 80. It isn't the gap between the two exits.
wrong.Nothing, same result: Exercise captures the intrinsic value only. The time value is lost.
wrong.$11.50, the whole premium: Exercising isn't worth zero. It still nets the $10 of intrinsic value.

conflicts: How sure the sources are that at the money holds the most time value: CME Group says time value 'will always be greatest' at the money; the OCC disclosure document says 'normally' (f15, f41) and OIC says deep ITM and far OTM have 'less time premium'. The file keys it as 'usually' (q10) and never as 'always'.

CME Group's moneyness page is written for options on futures ('future contract price'); its definitions match the OIC and OCC ones for stock options, and every key it supports also cites a Tier 1 fact.

Whether an option can trade below intrinsic value before expiry: CME Group's (futures options) page says the option value 'will always be greater than the intrinsic value until it reaches expiration'; the OCC disclosure document says an American-style option 'occasionally' trades below it. q27 keys the Tier 1 disclosure document and cites no CME fact for that point.
